## Appendix G Distance bounds for lifted product codes

In this appendix we prove upper bounds on the distance of a lifted product code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ in terms of algebraic properties of its base matrices $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ and of the group $G$ . The starting point is Theorem 7: whenever the binary matrices $L(A)$ and $R(B)$ have full row rank — which holds in particular under the square invertibility condition of Definition 16, and hence for every base matrix used in this paper (Remark 9) — the distances of the two classical base codes upper-bound the quantum distance. Any construction of a low-weight classical codeword therefore caps the quantum distance, and the rest of the appendix gives three such constructions. The commutator subgroup bound builds a codeword from the sum over the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ and is strongest when $G$ is close to abelian. The element-order bound applies whenever some entry of a base matrix has the form $1+g$ , in which case the distance is at most the order of $g$ . Finally, for abelian $G$ the base codes are classical quasi-cyclic LDPC codes, and we adapt the permanent-based distance bounds known for that family. These abelian bounds are tight: searching with our processor discovery pipeline and the distance estimation algorithm sQetch (Appendix H), we find a $\llbracket 560,112,\leq 14\rrbracket$ code that attains the distance- $14$ ceiling for $2\times 4$ base matrices of check weight at most $9$ .

### A Classical and quantum code distance

In this section we prove that the minimum distance of the two classical base codes $A$ and $B$ upper-bounds the distance of the lifted product code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ provided $L(A)$ and $R(B)$ have full row rank. We also show that the full row rank condition cannot be removed in general by exhibiting a counterexample where the classical base codes are not full row rank and have distance less than the lifted product code. The precise statement is the following.

#### Theorem 7 (Classical distance upper bound of quantum distance).

Let $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ for a finite group $G$ , and let $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ and $B\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{2}\times c_{2}}$ with $r_{1}<c_{1}$ and $r_{2}<c_{2}$ . Assume that the binary matrices

$$ L(A)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{1}|G|\times c_{1}|G|}\qquad\text{and}\qquad R(B)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{2}|G|\times c_{2}|G|} $$

have full row rank. Define the classical distances of the two base codes,

$$ d_{A}=\min\bigl\{\operatorname{wt}(u):0\neq u\in\ker L(A)\bigr\},\qquad d_{B}=\min\bigl\{\operatorname{wt}(v):0\neq v\in\ker R(B)\bigr\}, $$

where $\operatorname{wt}(\cdot)$ is the Hamming weight of a binary vector. Let $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ be the check matrices of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ (Definition 10), and define

$$ \begin{split}d_{x}&=\min\bigl\{\operatorname{wt}(x):x\in\ker H_{Z}\setminus\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{X})\bigr\},\\
d_{z}&=\min\bigl\{\operatorname{wt}(z):z\in\ker H_{X}\setminus\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{Z})\bigr\},\end{split} $$

where $\operatorname{rowspace}(H)$ is the linear space spanned by the row of $H$ , and $d_{Q}=\min(d_{x},d_{z})$ . Then

$$ d_{x}\leq d_{B},\qquad d_{z}\leq d_{A}, $$

and hence

$$ d_{Q}\leq\min(d_{A},d_{B}). $$

#### Remark 9.

Note that the square invertibility condition of Definition 16 is a special case of the full row rank condition, and so Theorem 7 applies to all codes we search for in this paper.

We will prove $d_{x}\leq d_{B}$ by exhibiting an explicit logical $X$ operator $X^{\star}$ of weight $d_{B}$ ; the bound $d_{z}\leq d_{A}$ follows from an almost identical argument. The physical qubits of a lifted product code come in two blocks, of sizes $c_{1}c_{2}|G|$ and $r_{1}r_{2}|G|$ , and so the support of an $X$ or $Z$ type Pauli operator over these physical qubits is naturally described as a pair of matrices over the group algebra $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , of shapes $c_{1}\times c_{2}$ and $r_{1}\times r_{2}$ respectively (Lemma 7 below makes this precise). In this language the candidate operator $X^{\star}$ is easy to describe: take a minimum-weight codeword of the classical base code $B$ and place it in a single row of the $c_{1}\times c_{2}$ matrix, setting all other entries, and the entire $r_{1}\times r_{2}$ matrix to zero. The weight of $X^{\star}$ is then $d_{B}$ by construction, and it is straightforward to check that it commutes with all the $Z$ stabilizers.

The real content of the proof is showing that the candidate $X^{\star}$ is not simply a product of $X$ stabilizers. The remainder of this section develops the proof in two steps. We first recast $X$ and $Z$ type Pauli operators on the physical qubits as pairs of matrices over $\mathcal{R}$ (Lemma 7), so that we may work over the ring for the remainder of the proof. We then show that the full row rank condition allows us to always construct such a candidate that is not a product of $X$ stabilizers (Lemma 8).

Over the ring, the minimum-distance codewords of the two classical base codes come from the kernels of the base matrices,

$$ K_{A}\coloneqq\{u\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}:Au=0\},\qquad K_{B}\coloneqq\{v\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times c_{2}}:vB^{*}=0\}. $$

In binary coordinates, Proposition 2(i) gives $\ker L(A)=\{\mathtt{b}(u):u\in K_{A}\}$ and $\ker R(B)=\{\mathtt{b}(v):v\in K_{B}\}$ , so $d_{A}$ and $d_{B}$ are the minimum weights of $\mathtt{b}(u)$ and $\mathtt{b}(v)$ over nonzero $u\in K_{A}$ and $v\in K_{B}$ , respectively.

To describe how we will construct logical operators from these minimum-weight codewords, it will be helpful to express $X$ and $Z$ type Pauli operators on $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ as pairs of matrices over $\mathcal{R}$ . The physical qubits of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ come in two blocks, of sizes $c_{1}c_{2}|G|$ and $r_{1}r_{2}|G|$ , so an $X$ or $Z$ type Pauli operator is described by a binary vector split across these two blocks. Since the checks are built from Kronecker products, they act most simply when each block of this vector is arranged as a matrix. Accordingly, we arrange the first block as $V\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times c_{2}}$ and the second as $U\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times r_{2}}$ , so that the full binary vector is $\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr)$ , where $\operatorname{vec}$ denotes the row-major flattening of (31). In this form, the checks act by left and right matrix multiplication.

#### Lemma 7 (Kernels and row spaces over the ring).

Let $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ be the check matrices of the lifted product code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ as in Definition 10. Then the map $(V,U)\mapsto\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr)$ is an $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear bijection from $\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times c_{2}}\oplus\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times r_{2}}$ onto $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{(c_{1}c_{2}+r_{1}r_{2})|G|}$ , under which:

- (i) $\begin{aligned} t]{2}&\ker H_{X}&&=\bigl\{\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr):AV+UB=0\bigr\},\\ &\ker H_{Z}&&=\bigl\{\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr):VB^{*}+A^{*}U=0\bigr\};\end{aligned}$

- (ii) $\begin{aligned} t]{2}&\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{X})&&=\bigl\{\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(A^{*}S)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(SB^{*}))\bigr):S\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}\bigr\},\\ &\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{Z})&&=\bigl\{\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(TB)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(AT))\bigr):T\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times r_{2}}\bigr\}.\end{aligned}$

#### Proof.

The map is a bijection since it is the composition of the $\operatorname{vec}$ operator with the entrywise binary expansion $\mathtt{b}$ , both of which are $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear bijections. We prove the two $H_{X}$ statements; the $H_{Z}$ statements follow from the same argument applied to the blocks of $H_{Z}$ in (24).

The two blocks of $H_{X}$ in Definition 10 are tensor products with an identity factor, so Proposition 2 yields

$$ L(A\otimes I_{c_{2}})\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V))=\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(AV)),\qquad R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B^{*})\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))=\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(UB)), $$

and adding the two blocks gives

$$ H_{X}\,\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr)=\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(AV+UB)). $$

By (99) and the injectivity of $\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(\cdot))$ on the syndrome space $\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}$ , we have $H_{X}\,\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr)=0$ if and only if $AV+UB=0$ ; since every vector over the physical qubits is $\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(V)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(U))\bigr)$ for some pair $(V,U)$ , this proves (i).

For (ii), the row space of $H_{X}$ is the image of $H_{X}^{T}$ , and every binary vector in the $X$ -syndrome space $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{1}c_{2}|G|}$ equals $\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(S))$ for a unique $S\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}$ ; hence

$$ \operatorname{rowspace}(H_{X})=\bigl\{H_{X}^{T}\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(S)):S\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}\bigr\}. $$

Using $L(M)^{T}=L(M^{*})$ and $R(M)^{T}=R(M^{*})$ followed by $(M\otimes I)^{*}=M^{*}\otimes I$ and $(I\otimes N)^{*}=I\otimes N^{*}$ ,

$$ H_{X}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}L(A^{*}\otimes I_{c_{2}})\\[2.0pt]
R(I_{r_{1}}\otimes B)\end{bmatrix}, $$

so Proposition 2 gives $H_{X}^{T}\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(S))=\bigl(\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(A^{*}S)),\,\mathtt{b}(\operatorname{vec}(SB^{*}))\bigr)$ , and (ii) follows. ∎

In light of Lemma 7, we identify the space of physical qubits with $\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times c_{2}}\oplus\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times r_{2}}$ and regard $\ker H_{X}$ , $\ker H_{Z}$ , $\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{X})$ , $\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{Z})$ as ring-level sets. Working in this picture will allow us to construct our candidate logical operator and prove that it is indeed a logical operator and not a product of stabilizers.

Write $e_{i}$ for the $i$ -th standard basis vector of $\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}$ that has the identity element $e$ in the $i$ -th position and zeros elsewhere. For $g\in G$ and a row vector $v_{B}\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times c_{2}}$ , the product $e_{i}g\,v_{B}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times c_{2}}$ is the matrix whose $i$ -th row is $gv_{B}$ and whose remaining rows are zero; matrices of this form will correspond to the support of our candidate $X$ logical operators, which live entirely on the first block of physical qubits. By Lemma 7(ii), the products of $X$ stabilizers are exactly the pairs $(A^{*}S,\,SB^{*})$ with $S\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}$ , so if the pair $(e_{i}g\,v_{B},\,0)$ were a product of $X$ stabilizers, then $e_{i}g\,v_{B}=A^{*}S$ for some $S$ . The next lemma shows that the row index $i$ and the group element $g$ can always be chosen so that no such $S$ exists. Part (ii) of the lemma is the corresponding statement for the candidate $Z$ logical operators. Writing $f_{j}$ for the analogous $j$ -th standard basis row vector of $\mathcal{R}^{1\times c_{2}}$ , the candidate $(u_{A}\,gf_{j},\,0)$ carries the column $u_{A}g$ in its $j$ -th column, and the lemma chooses $j$ and $g$ so that it is not among the $Z$ stabilizer products $(TB,\,AT)$ , $T\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times r_{2}}$ .

#### Lemma 8 (Avoiding the stabilizers).

Suppose that $L(A)$ and $R(B)$ have full row rank, with $r_{1}<c_{1}$ and $r_{2}<c_{2}$ . Then:

- (i) for every nonzero row vector $v_{B}\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times c_{2}}$ there exists $i\in\{1,\dots,c_{1}\}$ and $g\in G$ such that $e_{i}g\,v_{B}\neq A^{*}S$ for any $S\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}$ ;

- (ii) for every nonzero column vector $u_{A}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}$ there exists $j\in\{1,\dots,c_{2}\}$ and $g\in G$ such that $u_{A}\,gf_{j}\neq TB$ for any $T\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times r_{2}}$ .

#### Proof.

We prove (i), the statement for $L(A)$ ; the proof of (ii) is similar but with the roles of left and right multiplication exchanged.

Since $L(A)$ is full row rank, Proposition 2(i) implies that the map $u\mapsto Au$ corresponding to left multiplication by $A$ is a surjective map from $\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}$ onto $\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}}$ . Let $e_{k}$ be the $k$ -th standard basis vector of $\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}}$ that has the identity element $e$ in the $k$ -th position and zeros elsewhere. By surjectivity we may choose preimages $s_{k}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}}$ with $As_{k}=e_{k}$ for $k=1,\dots,r_{1}$ ; collecting them as the columns of $S_{A}\in\mathcal{R}^{c_{1}\times r_{1}}$ gives $AS_{A}=I_{r_{1}}$ .

Since the involution reverses products, this implies $S_{A}^{*}A^{*}=I_{r_{1}}$ , so $P_{A}\coloneqq I_{c_{1}}-A^{*}S_{A}^{*}$ satisfies

$$ P_{A}A^{*}=A^{*}-A^{*}(S_{A}^{*}A^{*})=0,\qquad I_{c_{1}}=A^{*}S_{A}^{*}+P_{A}. $$

Since $P_{A}A^{*}=0$ , the projector $P_{A}$ annihilates every matrix of the form $A^{*}S$ . Hence, it suffices to find $i$ and $g$ such that $(P_{A}\,e_{i}g)\,v_{B}\neq 0$ , since then $e_{i}g\,v_{B}$ cannot equal $A^{*}S$ for any $S$ .

Suppose then, for contradiction, that $(P_{A}\,e_{i}g)\,v_{B}=0$ for every $i$ and $g$ . Form the orbit space

$$ M_{B}\coloneqq\mathcal{R}v_{B}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}\{gv_{B}:g\in G\}\subseteq\mathcal{R}^{1\times c_{2}}. $$

By associativity, $0=(P_{A}\,e_{i}g)\,v_{B}=(P_{A}e_{i})(gv_{B})$ for every $i$ and $g$ , and since the vectors $gv_{B}$ span $M_{B}$ ,

$$ (P_{A}e_{i})\,m=0\qquad\text{for every $i$ and every $m\in M_{B}$.} $$

Now view $M_{B}^{\oplus c_{1}}$ as the space of $c_{1}\times c_{2}$ matrices whose rows lie in $M_{B}$ . Any $V\in M_{B}^{\oplus c_{1}}$ can be written as $V=\sum_{i=1}^{c_{1}}e_{i}m_{i}$ with $m_{i}\in M_{B}$ . Since $P_{A}V=0$ by (101), substituting $I_{c_{1}}=A^{*}S_{A}^{*}+P_{A}$ from (100) gives

$$ V=I_{c_{1}}V=(A^{*}S_{A}^{*}+P_{A})V=A^{*}(S_{A}^{*}V). $$

Every row of $S_{A}^{*}V$ is a left $\mathcal{R}$ -linear combination of rows of $V$ , so it still lies in $M_{B}$ . Consequently, left multiplication by $A^{*}$ is a surjective map from $M_{B}^{\oplus r_{1}}$ onto $M_{B}^{\oplus c_{1}}$ . But this is impossible since $r_{1}<c_{1}$ . Hence, some pair $(i,g)$ satisfies $(P_{A}\,e_{i}g)\,v_{B}\neq 0$ , and the lemma follows. ∎

We can now assemble the proof of Theorem 7.

#### Proof of Theorem 7.

We work in the ring picture of Lemma 7 and first prove $d_{x}\leq d_{B}$ . Pick $v_{B}\in K_{B}$ such that $\operatorname{wt}(\mathtt{b}(v_{B}))=d_{B}$ . By Lemma 8(i) there exists $i\in\{1,\dots,c_{1}\}$ and $g\in G$ such that $e_{i}g\,v_{B}\neq A^{*}S$ for any $S\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{2}}$ . Set

$$ X^{\star}\coloneqq(e_{i}g\,v_{B},\;0). $$

We claim that $X^{\star}$ is a nontrivial logical $X$ operator of weight $d_{B}$ . First, $X^{\star}$ commutes with all the $Z$ stabilizers. Since $v_{B}\in K_{B}$ ,

$$ (e_{i}g\,v_{B})B^{*}+A^{*}\cdot 0=e_{i}g\,(v_{B}B^{*})=0, $$

so $X^{\star}\in\ker H_{Z}$ by Lemma 7(i). Second, $X^{\star}$ is not a product of $X$ stabilizers i.e. $X^{\star}\notin\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{X})$ . If it were, then by Lemma 7(ii) its first component $e_{i}gv_{B}$ would equal $A^{*}S$ for some $S$ , contradicting the choice of $i$ and $g$ . Hence $X^{\star}$ is a nontrivial logical $X$ operator. Finally, the matrix $e_{i}g\,v_{B}$ has a single nonzero row, equal to $gv_{B}$ , so in binary coordinates $\operatorname{wt}(X^{\star})=\operatorname{wt}(\mathtt{b}(gv_{B}))=\operatorname{wt}(\mathtt{b}(v_{B}))=d_{B}$ . Hence $d_{x}\leq d_{B}$ .

The bound $d_{z}\leq d_{A}$ follows from a similar argument, using Lemma 8(ii) to build

$$ Z^{\star}\coloneqq(u_{A}\,gf_{j},\;0) $$

from a minimum-weight $u_{A}\in K_{A}$ . Combining the two bounds gives $d_{Q}=\min(d_{x},d_{z})\leq\min(d_{A},d_{B})$ . ∎

#### Remark 10.

One might hope to prove an unconditional statement about the classical distance upper bounding the quantum distance of the lifted product code. However, we present a counterexample that demonstrates this is not possible and that one cannot in general get rid of the full row rank condition in Theorem 7.

Let $G=C_{4}\times C_{2}=\langle x,y\mid x^{4}=y^{2}=e,\ xy=yx\rangle$ , so that $|G|=8$ , let $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , and consider the base matrices $A,B\in\mathcal{R}^{3\times 4}$ given by

$$ \displaystyle A \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}1+x+xy+x^{3}y&1+y+xy+x^{2}+x^{3}&1+xy+x^{2}y&x+xy+x^{2}y+x^{3}\\[2.84526pt]
y+x^{2}+x^{2}y+x^{3}&1+x+x^{2}y&1+x^{2}y+x^{3}&1+y+x+xy+x^{3}+x^{3}y\\[2.84526pt]
1+y+x^{2}y+x^{3}y&1+y+x+x^{3}+x^{3}y&1+x+x^{2}y+x^{3}y&x+x^{3}+x^{3}y\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle B \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}xy+x^{2}y+x^{3}+x^{3}y&x+xy+x^{2}+x^{2}y+x^{3}&xy+x^{2}y&xy+x^{2}y+x^{3}\\[2.84526pt]
y+x+x^{2}+x^{3}&1+x+x^{3}&x+x^{2}+x^{3}+x^{3}y&x^{2}+x^{3}+x^{3}y\\[2.84526pt]
1+x+x^{3}y&y+x^{3}&y+x+xy+x^{3}y&1+xy+x^{2}+x^{3}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Both matrices have the strictly wide shape required by Theorem 7, with $r_{1}=r_{2}=3<4=c_{1}=c_{2}$ but do not satisfy the full row rank condition. Indeed, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}L(A)=22$ and $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}R(B)=23$ , both strictly smaller than $r_{1}|G|=r_{2}|G|=24$ . Constructing bases for $\ker L(A)$ and $\ker R(B)$ and enumerating all $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -linear combinations of the basis vectors, we find that the classical distances of the base codes are $d_{A}=d_{B}=8$ . Using integer programming, we then verified that the distance of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ is exactly $10$ , so $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ is a $\llbracket 200,13,10\rrbracket$ code with

$$ d_{Q}=10>8=d_{A}=d_{B}, $$

and the conclusion of Theorem 7 fails without the full row rank condition.

We obtained the above counterexample by a guided randomized search over rank-deficient $3\times 4$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ where $G=C_{4}\times C_{2}$ . Let $\Omega=\sum_{g\in G}g$ . Since $g\Omega=\Omega$ for every $g\in G$ , multiplying $\Omega$ by any group-algebra element containing an even number of group elements gives zero; hence, if every entry in one column of a base matrix has even weight, the vector supported on that column with entry $\Omega$ is a codeword of binary weight $|G|=8$ . In the matrices in the above counterexample this occurs in the first column of $A$ and the third column of $B$ , giving the codewords $u_{A}=e_{1}\Omega=(\Omega,\,0,\,0,\,0)^{T}\in K_{A}$ and $v_{B}=\Omega f_{3}=(0,\,0,\,\Omega,\,0)\in K_{B}$ . We sampled the remaining entries randomly and rejected a matrix unless exhaustive enumeration of its kernel showed that the planted codeword was its unique minimum-weight codeword. After pairing candidate matrices $A$ and $B$ , we rejected the pair whenever any of the candidate operators (102)–(103) was not a stabilizer. Since $g\Omega=\Omega$ , these candidate logical operators reduce to $X_{i}^{\star}=(e_{i}\Omega f_{3},0)$ and $Z_{j}^{\star}=(e_{1}\Omega f_{j},0)$ , and we checked they were stabilizers by solving $A^{*}S=e_{i}\Omega f_{3}$ and $SB^{*}=0$ , and $TB=e_{1}\Omega f_{j}$ and $AT=0$ , for every $i$ and $j$ . We constructed $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ and used an exhaustive search to verify that every operator in $\ker H_{X}$ and $\ker H_{Z}$ of weight at most $D=\max\{d_{A},d_{B}\}$ was a stabilizer, thereby certifying $d_{Q}>D$ . Finally, we verified the distance of $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ with integer programming.

### B The commutator subgroup bound

We begin by recalling the definition of a commutator subgroup and establishing a few key properties.

#### Definition 22 (Commutator and commutator subgroup).

Let $G$ be a finite group. For elements $g,h\in G$ , the commutator of $g$ and $h$ is

$$ [g,h]=g\,h\,g^{-1}\,h^{-1}. $$

The commutator subgroup (or derived subgroup) of $G$ is the subgroup generated by all commutators:

$$ [G,G]=\langle\,[g,h]:g,h\in G\,\rangle. $$

The commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ , and the quotient $G/[G,G]$ is the abelianization of $G$ . The group $G$ is abelian if and only if $[G,G]=\{e\}$ .

#### Definition 23 (Commutator subgroup sum).

Let $K=[G,G]$ denote the commutator subgroup of $G$ . Define the element

$$ \sigma=\sum_{k\in K}k\;\in\;\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]. $$

The following proposition collects the key algebraic properties of $\sigma$ that will be used in the distance analysis.

#### Proposition 3 (Properties of the commutator subgroup sum).

Let $G$ be a finite group with commutator subgroup $K=[G,G]$ , and let $\sigma=\sum_{k\in K}k\in\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ . Then:

- 1. $\sigma$ is central in $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , i.e. $g\sigma=\sigma g$ for all $g\in G$ .

- 2. For any $c\in K$ , $(1+c)\,\sigma=0$ .

- 3. For all $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , $(ab+ba)\,\sigma=0$ .

#### Proof.

(1) Since $K$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ , for any $g\in G$ we have $gKg^{-1}=K$ , so $gK=Kg$ as sets. Therefore

$$ g\sigma=\sum_{k\in K}gk=\sum_{k^{\prime}\in gK}k^{\prime}=\sum_{k^{\prime}\in Kg}k^{\prime}=\sum_{k\in K}kg=\sigma g. $$

(2) For $c\in K$ , left multiplication by $c$ is a bijection on $K$ , so $c\sigma=\sum_{k\in K}ck=\sum_{k^{\prime}\in K}k^{\prime}=\sigma$ . Hence $(1+c)\sigma=\sigma+c\sigma=\sigma+\sigma=0$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ .

(3) It suffices to verify the identity on group elements $g,h\in G$ , since the general case follows by bilinearity. The commutator identity $gh=[g,h]\,hg$ gives

$$ (gh+hg)\,\sigma=\bigl(1+[g,h]\bigr)\,hg\,\sigma. $$

By part (1), $hg\sigma=\sigma hg$ , so

$$ \bigl(1+[g,h]\bigr)\,hg\,\sigma=\bigl(1+[g,h]\bigr)\,\sigma\,hg=0, $$

where the last equality uses part (2) with $c=[g,h]\in K$ . For general $a=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}g_{i}$ and $b=\sum_{j}\beta_{j}h_{j}$ in $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , bilinearity gives

$$ (ab+ba)\,\sigma=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{i}\beta_{j}\,(g_{i}h_{j}+h_{j}g_{i})\,\sigma=0. $$

∎

We now apply this algebraic machinery to bound the minimum distance of classical codes defined over the group algebra. Let $A\in\mathcal{R}^{r_{1}\times c_{1}}$ be a matrix over $\mathcal{R}=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ . Define the lifted classical code associated with $A$ as the binary linear code with parity-check matrix

$$ A_{L}=L(A), $$

and let $d_{A_{L}}$ denote its minimum distance. That is, $d_{A_{L}}$ is the minimum Hamming weight of a nonzero vector $u\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{c_{1}|G|}$ satisfying $L(A)\,u=0$ .

#### Proposition 4 (Commutator distance bound).

Let $G$ be a finite group with commutator subgroup $K=[G,G]$ , and let $\sigma=\sum_{k\in K}k$ . Let $A=[a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}]\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times m}$ with $a_{i}=\sum_{g\in I_{i}}g$ for index sets $I_{i}\subseteq G$ . Then for any pair $1\leq i<j\leq m$ such that $a_{i}\,\sigma\neq 0$ or $a_{j}\,\sigma\neq 0$ ,

$$ d_{A_{L}}\leq(|I_{i}|+|I_{j}|)\cdot|K|. $$

#### Proof.

Define $w\in\mathcal{R}^{m}$ by $w_{i}=a_{j}\,\sigma$ , $w_{j}=a_{i}\,\sigma$ , and $w_{\ell}=0$ for $\ell\notin\{i,j\}$ . Let $\tilde{w}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m|G|}$ denote the binary vector obtained by expanding each entry $w_{\ell}\in\mathcal{R}$ into its coefficient vector in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{|G|}$ . We claim that $\tilde{w}$ is a nonzero codeword of $A_{L}$ . Since $A$ has a single row, $A_{L}\tilde{w}$ is the binary expansion of $Aw=\sum_{\ell}a_{\ell}w_{\ell}$ . Computing:

$$ L(A)\tilde{w}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}a_{\ell}w_{\ell}=a_{i}w_{i}+a_{j}w_{j}=a_{i}a_{j}\,\sigma+a_{j}a_{i}\,\sigma=(a_{i}a_{j}+a_{j}a_{i})\,\sigma=0, $$

where the last equality follows from Proposition 3(3).

All that remains is to bound the weight of $\tilde{w}$ . Write $w_{i}=a_{j}\,\sigma=\sum_{g\in I_{j}}g\sigma=\sum_{g\in I_{j}}\sum_{k\in K}gk$ . The elements $gk$ for $k\in K$ form the coset $gK$ , so $a_{j}\,\sigma=\sum_{g\in I_{j}}\mathbf{1}_{gK}$ , where $\mathbf{1}_{gK}$ denotes the formal sum of elements in $gK$ . Over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ , group elements appearing an even number of times in the sum cancel, so $\operatorname{wt}_{G}(w_{i})\leq|I_{j}|\cdot|K|$ . Similarly $\operatorname{wt}_{G}(w_{j})\leq|I_{i}|\cdot|K|$ . Hence

$$ d_{A_{L}}\leq\operatorname{wt}(\tilde{w})=\operatorname{wt}_{G}(w_{i})+\operatorname{wt}_{G}(w_{j})\leq(|I_{j}|+|I_{i}|)\cdot|K|.\qed $$

#### Remark 11.

For groups of the form $G=C_{N}\times G^{\prime}$ where $G^{\prime}$ is nonabelian, the commutator subgroup is $K=[G,G]=\{e\}\times[G^{\prime},G^{\prime}]$ , since $C_{N}$ is abelian. In this case $|K|=|[G^{\prime},G^{\prime}]|$ , and the bound from Proposition 4 becomes $d_{A_{L}}\leq(|I_{i}|+|I_{j}|)\cdot|[G^{\prime},G^{\prime}]|$ .

### C The element order bound

A single weight-two entry in a base matrix already caps the distance by the order of a group element.

#### Definition 24 (Order of a group element).

Let $G$ be a group and $g\in G$ . The order of $g$ , denoted $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ , is the smallest positive integer $n$ such that

$$ g^{n}=e, $$

where $e$ is the identity of $G$ . If no such $n$ exists, we set $\operatorname{ord}(g)=\infty$ . Equivalently, $\operatorname{ord}(g)=|\langle g\rangle|$ , the order of the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$ .

#### Theorem 8 (Element-order bound).

Let $A\in\mathcal{R}^{1\times n_{a}}$ have an entry equal to $1+g$ for some $g\in G$ . Then $\ker(L(A))$ contains a nonzero codeword of Hamming weight $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ , so the classical distance is at most $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ ; by Theorem 7, the quantum code $\operatorname{LP}(A,B)$ then satisfies $d_{Q}\leq\operatorname{ord}(g)$ .

#### Proof.

Say the entry is $a_{j}=1+g$ . Any $r\in\mathcal{R}$ with $(1+g)\,r=0$ , placed in coordinate $j$ and padded with zeros, is a codeword of $\ker(L(A))$ , since the single row evaluates to $a_{j}r=(1+g)r=0$ . Writing $r=\sum_{h\in G}a_{h}\,h$ ,

$$ (1+g)\,r=\sum_{h\in G}\bigl(a_{h}+a_{g^{-1}h}\bigr)\,h=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_{gh}=a_{h}\ \ \text{for all }h\in G, $$

so the coefficients of $r$ are constant on the orbits of left multiplication by $g$ . These orbits are the right cosets of $\langle g\rangle$ ,

$$ \mathcal{O}_{h}=\{\,h,\;gh,\;g^{2}h,\;\ldots,\;g^{\operatorname{ord}(g)-1}h\,\}, $$

each of size $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ . Hence every solution is a sum of orbit indicators $\hat{\mathcal{O}}_{i}\coloneqq\sum_{k=0}^{\operatorname{ord}(g)-1}g^{k}h_{i}$ , and its weight lies in $\{0,\operatorname{ord}(g),2\operatorname{ord}(g),\ldots,|G|\}$ . The lightest nonzero choice, a single orbit, has weight $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ , which bounds the distance. ∎

### D Distance bounds on classical quasi-cyclic LDPC codes

By the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, every finite abelian group is a direct product of cyclic groups. In the univariate case the classical base codes are the well-studied quasi-cyclic LDPC codes, where $G=\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]\cong\mathbb{F}_{2}[x]/(x^{\ell}-1)$ . Therefore, each entry of the $m_{a}\times n_{a}$ base matrix $A$ is a polynomial $A_{ij}(x)$ of degree less than $\ell$ , and the classical code is the binary kernel $\mathcal{C}_{A}=\ker(A_{\mathrm{bin}})$ with $A_{\mathrm{bin}}=L[A]$ ; we write $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})$ for its minimum distance. Since $G$ is abelian, the left and right regular representations coincide and we need not distinguish them. Under the identification $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]^{n_{a}}\cong\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{a}\ell}$ , ring multiplication is realized by $L[\cdot]$ and the ring kernel embeds isometrically into the binary kernel, so the Hamming weight of a lift $\tilde{c}$ equals the sum of the ring weights of its components.

The rest of this subsection develops the classical distance bounds that let our pipeline discard unpromising base matrices before building any quantum code, exploiting the fact that the quantum distance never exceeds the classical one (Theorem 7). The development proceeds in two parts. First, we attach to each base matrix its integer weight matrix (Definition 25) and recall the permanent-based upper bounds on the binary distance $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})$ from [115, 116] (Theorems 9 and 10). These bounds expose a sharp dichotomy: monomial (weight-one) base matrices cap the distance at $(m_{a}+1)!$ (Corollary 1), whereas polynomial entries are exactly what break this ceiling (Remark 14), which is why our search uses polynomial entries. We then formalize the check weight of the lifted product code (Definition 26) and combine it with the permanent bound to prove our main result: every $2\times 4$ base matrix of check weight at most $9$ yields an LP code of distance at most $14$ (Theorem 12).

#### 1 Weight-matrix bound

#### Definition 25 (Weight matrix of a QC-LDPC code).

The weight matrix of $A$ is the integer matrix

$$ W(A)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{m_{a}\times n_{a}},\qquad W(A)_{ij}\;\triangleq\;\#\bigl\{\,g\in G\;:\;\text{coefficient of }g\text{ in }A_{ij}(x)\text{ equals }1\,\bigr\}, $$

i.e. each entry records the number of monomials in the corresponding polynomial. Following [115], we call $A$ monomial (or of type- $1$ ) if $W(A)_{ij}\leq 1$ for all $i,j$ , and of type- $M$ more generally with $M=\max_{ij}W(A)_{ij}$ .

#### Lemma 9 (Permanent codeword construction [115]).

For any column subset $S\subseteq[n_{a}]$ of size $|S|=m_{a}+1$ , the ring vector $c\in(\mathbb{F}_{2}[G])^{n_{a}}$ defined by

$$ c_{j}\;=\;\begin{cases}\operatorname{perm}\!\bigl(A_{[m_{a}],\,S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr),&j\in S,\\[2.0pt]
0,&j\notin S,\end{cases} $$

where $A_{[m_{a}],T}$ denotes the $m_{a}\times|T|$ submatrix on columns $T$ and the permanent is taken over the commutative ring $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , satisfies $Ac=0$ . Consequently, its lift $\tilde{c}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n_{a}\ell}$ is a binary codeword of $\mathcal{C}_{A}$ with Hamming weight

$$ \mathrm{wt}_{H}(\tilde{c})\;=\;\sum_{j\in S}\mathrm{wt}\!\bigl(\operatorname{perm}\!\bigl(A_{[m_{a}],S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr)\bigr). $$

#### Proof.

For each row $i\in[m_{a}]$ , expanding by cofactors along the row $A_{i,S}$ gives

$$ (Ac)_{i}\;=\;\sum_{j\in S}A_{ij}\operatorname{perm}\!\bigl(A_{[m_{a}],S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr)\;=\;\operatorname{perm}\!\begin{bmatrix}A_{i,S}\\
A_{[m_{a}],S}\end{bmatrix}\;=\;0, $$

because in characteristic $2$ the permanent equals the determinant, and a determinant with a repeated row vanishes (row $i$ of $A_{[m_{a}],S}$ already appears below). The weight identity (115) then follows from the isometry $\mathrm{wt}_{H}(\tilde{c})=\sum_{j}\mathrm{wt}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]}(c_{j})$ recorded above. ∎

#### Remark 12.

This codeword construction relies only on the commutativity of the group. Although it is usually stated for QC-LDPC codes over a cyclic group, it therefore holds for any abelian group, including the direct product of two cyclic groups considered here, so every bound below that rests on it generalizes immediately to linear codes over abelian groups.

Minimising the right-hand side of (115) over admissible $S$ with $\min^{*}$ skipping the trivial all-zero codeword by returning the smallest nonzero value of the sum yields the two upper bounds that will be used throughout.

#### Theorem 9 (Polynomial permanent bound [115, Thm. 7]).

The minimum distance of the QC-LDPC code $\mathcal{C}_{A}$ satisfies

$$ d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\;\leq\;\min^{*}_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n_{a}]\\
|S|=m_{a}+1\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{j\in S}\mathrm{wt}\!\bigl(\operatorname{perm}\!\bigl(A_{[m_{a}],S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr)\bigr), $$

where the weight of each ring permanent reflects the $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -cancellations among the monomials in its support.

#### Theorem 10 (Weight-matrix permanent bound [115, Thm. 8], [116, Thm. 2]).

With $W(A)$ the integer weight matrix of Definition 25,

$$ d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\;\leq\;\min^{*}_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n_{a}]\\
|S|=m_{a}+1\end{subarray}}\;\sum_{j\in S}\operatorname{perm}\!\bigl(W(A)_{[m_{a}],\,S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr), $$

the right-hand permanents being ordinary integer permanents of $m_{a}\times m_{a}$ submatrices.

#### Proof.

The crude inequality $\mathrm{wt}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]}(\operatorname{perm}(M))\leq\operatorname{perm}(W(M))$ holds for any ring matrix $M$ , since the right-hand side counts the total support of the permanent expansion before $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -cancellations. Applying this to each summand in (117) gives (118). ∎

#### Remark 13.

The bound of Theorem 9 is tighter than that of Theorem 10; in practice we use the weight-matrix bound of Theorem 10 to choose an ansatz and the polynomial bound of Theorem 9 as a finer filter.

#### Corollary 1 (Factorial bound for monomial $A$ [115, Cor. 9], [116, Thm. 1]).

If $A$ is monomial, then

$$ d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\;\leq\;(m_{a}+1)!. $$

#### Proof.

When $A$ is monomial, every entry of $A_{[m_{a}],S\setminus\{j\}}$ is a single group element, so

$$ \operatorname{perm}\!\bigl(A_{[m_{a}],S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr)\;=\;\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Sym}(m_{a})}\,\prod_{i=1}^{m_{a}}A_{i,\sigma(i)} $$

is a sum of $m_{a}!$ monomials with $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -weight at most $m_{a}!$ . Summing over the $m_{a}+1$ indices in $S$ in (115) bounds the right-hand side by $(m_{a}+1)\cdot m_{a}!=(m_{a}+1)!$ , and minimising over $S$ in Theorem 9 yields (119). ∎

#### Remark 14 (The monomial ceiling and the role of polynomial entries).

Corollary 1 caps monomial QC-LDPC codes at $d\leq 6$ for $m_{a}=2$ , $d\leq 24$ for $m_{a}=3$ , and $d\leq 120$ for $m_{a}=4$ , irrespective of the lifting factor $\ell$ . Polynomial entries are the lever that breaks this ceiling: each weight- $w$ entry contributes $w$ rather than $1$ monomials to the permanent expansion, so the right-hand side of (118) can scale up to $(m_{a}+1)!\cdot\prod_{ij}W(A)_{ij}$ in the worst case, while (117) can shrink it further only through $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ -cancellations among those monomials. Concretely, [115] exhibits a type- $2$ $(3,4)$ -regular QC-LDPC code with $d=32>24=(3+1)!$ and a type- $3$ one with $d=54$ at the same regularity. Our pipeline therefore samples over polynomial entries from the outset, restricted only by the desired check weight and by the girth obstructions of Theorem 11 below.

#### Theorem 11 (Girth bounds from weight-matrix substructure [115, Thm. 18]).

Let $g(A_{\mathrm{bin}})$ denote the girth of the Tanner graph of $A_{\mathrm{bin}}$ . Whenever $W(A)$ admits one of the substructures below (modulo row and column permutations and transposition), the girth is bounded accordingly:

$$ [\,3\,]\;\Rightarrow\;g\leq 6,\qquad[\,2,\;2\,]\;\Rightarrow\;g\leq 8,\qquad\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\
1&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\;\Rightarrow\;g\leq 10,\qquad\bigl[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&1\\
1&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr]\;\Rightarrow\;g\leq 12. $$

#### Definition 26 (Check weight of the LP code).

For a weight matrix $W(A)$ , write $R_{i}(A)\coloneqq\sum_{j}W(A)_{ij}$ and $C_{j}(A)\coloneqq\sum_{i}W(A)_{ij}$ for its row and column sums. The check weight of the lifted product code built from $(A,B)$ is the largest Hamming weight of any stabilizer generator; using $\max_{i,j}\bigl(f(i)+g(j)\bigr)=\max_{i}f(i)+\max_{j}g(j)$ , it equals

$$ w_{\mathrm{ch}}(A,B)\;=\;\max\!\Bigl\{\,\max_{i}R_{i}(A)+\max_{j}C_{j}(B),\;\;\max_{j}C_{j}(A)+\max_{i}R_{i}(B)\,\Bigr\}. $$

In the abelian case $B=A$ this reduces to $w_{\mathrm{ch}}=R+C$ , where $R\coloneqq\max_{i}R_{i}(A)$ and $C\coloneqq\max_{j}C_{j}(A)$ .

#### Theorem 12 (Distance ceiling for LP codes at check weight $\leq 9$ with $2\times 4$ classical base matrix).

Let $A$ be a $2\times 4$ ring matrix over a commutative group algebra $\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]$ , paired with itself ( $B=A$ ) in the LP construction. Write $W=W(A)$ , $R_{i}\coloneqq\sum_{j}W_{ij}$ , $C_{j}\coloneqq\sum_{i}W_{ij}$ , and set

$$ R\;\coloneqq\;\max_{i\in\{0,1\}}R_{i},\qquad C\;\coloneqq\;\max_{j\in\{0,1,2,3\}}C_{j}. $$

If the check weight of the LP code satisfies

$$ w_{\mathrm{ch}}\;=\;\max_{(i_{a},i_{b})\in\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2,3\}}\!\bigl(R_{i_{a}}+C_{i_{b}}\bigr)\;=\;R+C\;\leq\;9, $$

Then the distance of the LP code satisfies $d_{q}\leq 14$ .

#### Proof.

We prove it by showing that the classical QC-LDPC code $\mathcal{C}_{A}=\ker(A_{\mathrm{bin}})$ satisfies $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 14$ ; since $d_{q}\leq d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})$ , this gives $d_{q}\leq 14$ .

For each size- $3$ column subset $S\subset\{0,1,2,3\}$ write

$$ \operatorname{perm}_{S}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in S}\operatorname{perm}\bigl(W_{\{0,1\},\,S\setminus\{j\}}\bigr). $$

Set $D\coloneqq\sum_{i}W_{0i}W_{1i}\geq 0$ . Each unordered pair $\{i,j\}\subset\{0,1,2,3\}$ lies in exactly two of the $\binom{4}{3}=4$ size- $3$ subsets, and the $2\times 2$ permanent of columns $\{i,j\}$ equals $W_{0i}W_{1j}+W_{1i}W_{0j}$ , so

$$ \sum_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}=2\sum_{i<j}\bigl(W_{0i}W_{1j}+W_{1i}W_{0j}\bigr)=2(R_{0}R_{1}-D), $$

where the last equality uses $\sum_{i\neq j}W_{0i}W_{1j}=R_{0}R_{1}-D$ . Hence

$$ \min^{*}_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}\;\leq\;\frac{1}{4}\sum_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}=\frac{R_{0}R_{1}-D}{2}. $$

Case 1: $R_{0}R_{1}-D\leq 28$ . Inequality (125) gives $\min^{*}_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}\leq 14$ , and Theorem 10 yields $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 14$ .

Case 2: $R_{0}R_{1}-D\geq 30$ . We show that the configurations satisfying this inequality together with (123) are extremely restricted, and in each one either $\min^{*}_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}\leq 14$ holds anyway or $A$ admits a size- $2$ codeword of Hamming weight $\leq 6$ .

In the following, we will focus on discussing the second case:

Since $D\geq 0$ , $R_{0}R_{1}\geq 30$ , and $R_{0},R_{1}\leq R$ implies $R^{2}\geq 30$ , so $R\geq 6$ . The total-weight identity gives $R_{0}+R_{1}=\sum_{j}C_{j}\leq 4C$ . Therefore,

$$ R_{0}R_{1}\leq\tfrac{(R_{0}+R_{1})^{2}}{4}\leq 4C^{2}, $$

hence $4C^{2}\geq 30$ , so $C\geq 3$ . As check-weight $w_{\mathrm{ch}}=R+C\leq 9$ and $R_{0}R_{1}\geq 29$ , the only possible configuration is $R=6$ and $C=3$ .

Since $R_{0}+R_{1}\geq 2\sqrt{R_{0}R_{1}}\geq 2\sqrt{30}>10$ and $R_{0}+R_{1}\leq 4C=12$ , the only possibilities are $R_{0}+R_{1}\in\{11,12\}$ , which we treat in turn.

For $R_{0}+R_{1}=11$ , without loss of generality, we assume $R_{0}=5$ , $R_{1}=6$ , so $R_{0}R_{1}=30$ and the constraint $R_{0}R_{1}-D\geq 30$ gives $D=0$ . The only column multiset consistent with $R_{0}=5$ , $R_{1}=6$ , $D=0$ , and $\max_{j}C_{j}=3$ is $\{(3,0)^{\top},(2,0)^{\top},(0,3)^{\top},(0,3)^{\top}\}$ . Direct computation on this multiset gives the triplet-sum multiset $\{12,15,15,18\}$ , so $\min^{*}_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}=12$ and Theorem 10 yields $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 12<14$ .

For $R_{0}+R_{1}=12$ , as each row sum $\leq R=6$ , then $R_{0}=R_{1}=6$ . Also since $\sum_{j}C_{j}=12=4C$ each column sum is exactly $3$ . Let $w_{i}\coloneqq W_{0i}\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ , we have $W_{1i}=3-w_{i}$ and $\sum_{i}w_{i}=6$ . The partitions of $6$ into four ordered parts in $\{0,1,2,3\}$ are, up to permutation, the five listed below where in each case $D=18-\sum_{i}w_{i}^{2}$ , and the multi-set of the four triplet sums $\{\operatorname{perm}_{S}\}_{|S|=3}$ is invariant under permutations of $W$ ’s columns, so a direct computation on a single representative gives:

| $(w_{i})$ partition | $D$ | $\{\operatorname{perm}_{S}\}_{\|S\|=3}$ | $\min^{*}_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(2,2,1,1)$ | $8$ | $\{14,14,14,14\}$ | $14$ |
| $(3,2,1,0)$ | $4$ | $\{14,14,18,18\}$ | $14$ |
| $(2,2,2,0)$ | $6$ | $\{12,16,16,16\}$ | $12$ |
| $(3,1,1,1)$ | $6$ | $\{12,16,16,16\}$ | $12$ |
| $(3,3,0,0)$ | $0$ | $\{18,18,18,18\}$ | $18$ |

For the first four partitions, $\min^{*}_{S}\operatorname{perm}_{S}\leq 14$ , so Theorem 10 directly gives $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 14$ . The remaining partition $(3,3,0,0)$ has $D=0$ , which forces $W_{0i}W_{1i}=0$ for every $i$ : each column of $W$ has at most one nonzero entry, and with $R_{0}=R_{1}=6$ and column sums $3$ , the matrix $W$ is, up to column permutation,

$$ W=\begin{pmatrix}3&3&0&0\\
0&0&3&3\end{pmatrix}. $$

The Tanner graph of a code with this $W$ splits into at least two connected components, and a codeword supported on a single component, which corresponds to a $1\times 2$ check matrix, already bounds the distance of the whole code. As each connected component corresponds to a check matrix $A^{sub}$ with weight matrix

$$ W_{sub}=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\end{pmatrix}, $$

applying the distance bound on it gives

$$ d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq d(A^{sub}_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 3+3=6<14. $$

Combining all these cases, we have $d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 14$ . Thus,

$$ d_{q}\leq d(A_{\mathrm{bin}})\leq 14. $$

This completes the proof. ∎

## Appendix H sQetch: A fast GPU-based CSS-code distance estimator

We introduce sQetch [61], a very fast GPU-based algorithm for estimating the minimum distance of a quantum CSS code. Like the QDistRnd estimator [106], sQetch is a form of random information-set decoding (ISD). Its key ingredient is that each trial operates on a random low-dimensional sketch of a check-matrix null space rather than on the full null space. This both reduces the cost per trial and maps naturally to GPU shared memory. On a single NVIDIA RTX 5090, sQetch achieves a speedup of roughly $100{,}000\times$ over the CPU-based QDistRnd baseline, making it feasible to explore the vast design space of high-rate fault-tolerant processors, in which viable candidates are extremely sparse. The same estimator also offers significant acceleration in the search over surgery gadgets and the estimation of circuit-level distance.

### A Notation

We consider a quantum CSS code with parameters $\llbracket n,k\rrbracket$ and check matrices $H_{X},H_{Z}$ satisfying $H_{X}H_{Z}^{\top}=0$ (Appendix A). Its distance is $d=\min(d_{x},d_{z})$ . Here, $d_{x}$ is the minimum Hamming weight of a nontrivial logical $X$ operator, namely a vector in $\ker(H_{Z})\setminus\rowspan(H_{X})$ , whereas $d_{z}$ is the minimum Hamming weight of a nontrivial logical $Z$ operator, namely a vector in $\ker(H_{X})\setminus\rowspan(H_{Z})$ , as defined in Appendix G. Let the null spaces be:

$$ \mathcal{N}_{x}\coloneqq\ker(H_{X}),\qquad\mathcal{N}_{z}\coloneqq\ker(H_{Z}), $$

with dimensions

$$ \nu_{x}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{N}_{x})=n-\rank(\Hx),\qquad\nu_{z}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{N}_{z})=n-\rank(\Hz), $$

respectively. After fixing a basis for each null space, let $N_{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\nu_{x}\times n}$ and $N_{z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\nu_{z}\times n}$ be the matrices whose rows are these basis vectors. Thus,

$$ \rowspan(N_{x})=\mathcal{N}_{x},\qquad\rowspan(N_{z})=\mathcal{N}_{z}. $$

Because $\ker(N_{z})=\rowspan(H_{Z})$ , a vector $v\in\mathcal{N}_{x}$ represents a nontrivial logical $Z$ operator exactly when $N_{z}v\neq 0$ . Similarly, a vector $u\in\mathcal{N}_{z}$ represents a nontrivial logical $X$ operator exactly when $N_{x}u\neq 0$ . Therefore, sQetch searches over

$$ \begin{split}d_{x}&=\min\bigl\{\operatorname{wt}(u):u\in\mathcal{N}_{z},\ N_{x}u\neq 0\bigr\},\\
d_{z}&=\min\bigl\{\operatorname{wt}(v):v\in\mathcal{N}_{x},\ N_{z}v\neq 0\bigr\}.\end{split} $$

Recall that

$$ k=n-\rank(\Hx)-\rank(\Hz). $$

Since $\nu_{x}=k+\rank(\Hz)$ , and symmetrically $\nu_{z}=k+\rank(\Hx)$ , both null-space dimensions satisfy $\nu_{x},\nu_{z}\geq k$ .

#### Remark 16.

If $H_{Z}=0$ , estimating $d_{z}$ reduces to estimating the distance of the classical code with parity-check matrix $H_{X}$ .

### B The sQetch algorithm

Computing the exact distance of a general linear code is NP-hard [117, 118]. Instead, sQetch performs many random trials biased toward low-weight codewords. Every nontrivial logical operator found in this way gives an upper bound on the distance, and the running estimate decreases whenever a lower-weight operator is found. The heuristic is co-designed with the GPU. Without loss of generality, we describe the estimation of $d_{z}$ ; the same procedure estimates $d_{x}$ after exchanging $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ .

Our goal is to find the lowest-weight vector in $\ker(H_{X})$ that is not in $\operatorname{rowspace}(H_{Z})$ . Starting from a matrix whose rows form a basis of $\ker(H_{X})$ , we randomly shuffle its columns and put it in reduced row echelon form (RREF), which biases the rows toward low weight vectors by forcing zeros in the pivot columns. sQetch follows the same idea but samples only a few random basis vectors in each trial, so the working matrix fits cheaply in GPU shared memory.

Concretely, the null-space matrix $N_{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{\nu_{x}\times n}$ , satisfying $\rowspan(N_{x})=\mathcal{N}_{x}$ , is computed once. Each trial forms a random $\kappa$ -row sketch $\tilde{N}_{x}$ by sampling row indices independently and uniformly with replacement:

$$ i_{1},\ldots,i_{\kappa}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Unif}\bigl(\{0,\ldots,\nu_{x}-1\}\bigr),\qquad\tilde{N}_{x}[s,:]=N_{x}[i_{s},:],\quad s=1,\ldots,\kappa. $$

The GPU constructs $\gamma$ such sketches in parallel, each from an independent random seed. For each sketch $\tilde{N}_{x}^{(j)}$ , it samples a uniformly random permutation $\pi^{(j)}\in S_{n}$ , permutes the columns to obtain $\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime(j)}$ , and applies Gauss-Jordan elimination to obtain the row-reduced echelon form $\tilde{N}_{x,\mathrm{RREF}}^{\prime(j)}$ . Let $P_{\pi}^{(j)}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ denote its pivot columns and let

$$ F_{\pi}^{(j)}\coloneqq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\setminus P_{\pi}^{(j)} $$

denote its free columns. Every nonzero row $r$ of the row-reduced matrix has exactly one nonzero entry in $P_{\pi}^{(j)}$ ; all its remaining nonzero entries lie in $F_{\pi}^{(j)}$ . Hence,

$$ \operatorname{wt}(r)=1+\bigl|\supp(r)\cap F_{\pi}^{(j)}\bigr|. $$

Each nonzero row $r_{\ell}^{(j)}$ represents a vector in $\mathcal{N}_{x}$ and is a nontrivial logical $Z$ operator precisely when $N_{z}(r_{\ell}^{(j)})^{\top}\neq 0$ . Whenever such a row has weight below the current best value, sQetch lowers its estimate of $d_{z}$ . Algorithm H.B summarizes one trial.

Output: the lowest-weight nontrivial logical candidate $v^{\star}\in\mathcal{N}_{x}$ found in this trial and its weight $\hat{d_{z}}$ , or $(\bot,+\infty)$ if no such candidate is found; the algorithm also signals Found when $\hat{d_{z}}<d^{\star}$ . 1: $\pi\leftarrow\textsc{Fisher--Yates}(\{0,\ldots,n-1\})$ // uniform random column permutation 2: $i_{1},\ldots,i_{\kappa}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Unif}\bigl(\{0,\ldots,\nu_{x}-1\}\bigr)$ 3: $\tilde{N}_{x}\leftarrow\bigl[N_{x}[i_{s},:]\bigr]_{s=1}^{\kappa}$ // row sketch of $N_{x}$ 4: $\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}[:,c]\leftarrow\tilde{N}_{x}[:,\pi(c)]$ for $c=0,\ldots,n-1$ // permute columns 5: $\mathit{pr}\leftarrow 0$ 6: for $c=0,1,\ldots,n-1$ do // column-ordered Gauss–Jordan elimination 7: scan rows $r\in\{\mathit{pr},\ldots,\kappa-1\}$ for a $1$ in column $c$ of $\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}$ 8: if one is found in row $r^{\star}$ then 9: swap rows $r^{\star}\leftrightarrow\mathit{pr}$ of $\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}$ 10: for $r\in\{0,\ldots,\kappa-1\}$ with $r\neq\mathit{pr}$ do 11: if $\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}[r,c]=1$ then $\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}[r,:]\leftarrow\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}[r,:]\oplus\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}[\mathit{pr},:]$ 12: end for 13: $\mathit{pr}\leftarrow\mathit{pr}+1$ 14: end if 15: if $\mathit{pr}=\kappa$ then break 16: end for 17: $\tilde{N}_{x,\mathrm{RREF}}^{\prime}\leftarrow\tilde{N}_{x}^{\prime}$ 18: $\hat{d_{z}}\leftarrow+\infty;\;\;v^{\star}\leftarrow\bot$ 19: for each nonzero row $r^{\prime}$ of $\tilde{N}_{x,\mathrm{RREF}}^{\prime}$ do // undo permutation, test logical nontriviality, and compute weight 20: define $r\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ by $r[\pi(c)]\leftarrow r^{\prime}[c]$ for $c=0,\ldots,n-1$ 21: if $N_{z}r^{\top}\neq 0$ and $\operatorname{wt}(r)<\hat{d_{z}}$ then $\hat{d_{z}}\leftarrow\operatorname{wt}(r);\;\;v^{\star}\leftarrow r$ 22: end for 23: if $\hat{d_{z}}<d^{\star}$ then signal Found; return $v^{\star},\hat{d_{z}}$ 24: return $v^{\star},\hat{d_{z}}$

### C Hit-probability analysis

Consider a constant-rate CSS code, for which $\nu_{x}=\Theta(n)$ , and assume $d_{z}\ll n$ , as is typical in practice. Fix a minimum-weight nontrivial logical $Z$ operator $c^{\star}$ with $\operatorname{wt}(c^{\star})=d_{z}$ . Because the rows of $N_{x}$ form a basis, $c^{\star}$ has a unique expansion in these rows. Let $j^{\star}$ be the number of basis rows with nonzero coefficients in this expansion. The span of a $\kappa$ -row sketch contains $c^{\star}$ exactly when all $j^{\star}$ required basis rows are sampled at least once. Because the rows are sampled independently with replacement, inclusion–exclusion gives

$$ P_{\operatorname{sketch}}=\sum_{t=0}^{j^{\star}}(-1)^{t}\binom{j^{\star}}{t}\left(1-\frac{t}{\nu_{x}}\right)^{\kappa}. $$

When $j^{\star}\ll\kappa\ll\nu_{x}$ , the leading approximation is

$$ P_{\operatorname{sketch}}\approx\left(\frac{\kappa}{\nu_{x}}\right)^{j^{\star}}. $$

Conditioned on the sketch span containing $c^{\star}$ , the random column permutation exposes $c^{\star}$ as a row of $\tilde{N}_{x,\mathrm{RREF}}^{\prime}$ exactly when one element of $\supp(c^{\star})$ lies in the pivot set. Under the genericity assumptions that the sketch has full row rank and that its pivot set behaves as a uniformly random $\kappa$ -subset of the $n$ columns, the conditional hit probability is

$$ P\bigl(\mathrm{hit}\mid\operatorname{sketch}\bigr)\approx\frac{d_{z}\binom{n-d_{z}}{\kappa-1}}{\binom{n}{\kappa}}. $$

For $n\gg d_{z}$ , this becomes

$$ P\bigl(\mathrm{hit}\mid\operatorname{sketch}\bigr)\approx\frac{d_{z}\kappa}{n}\left(1-\frac{d_{z}}{n}\right)^{\kappa-1}. $$

Therefore,

$$ P_{\mathrm{hit}}=P\bigl(\mathrm{hit}\mid\operatorname{sketch}\bigr)P_{\operatorname{sketch}}\approx\left(\frac{\kappa}{\nu_{x}}\right)^{j^{\star}}\frac{d_{z}\kappa}{n}\left(1-\frac{d_{z}}{n}\right)^{\kappa-1}. $$

### D Benchmark

We benchmark sQetch against QDistRnd [106], a state-of-the-art CPU distance estimator, on the workload relevant to our high-rate qLDPC processor discovery pipeline. Figure 7 reports the wall-clock time required to screen approximately $10^{7}$ candidate codes using approximately $10^{5}$ random-ISD trials per code, or about $10^{12}$ trials in total. The benchmark compares a single GPU with a high-end CPU as a function of code size.

*Figure 7: Wall-clock time, in days on a logarithmic scale, required to screen approximately $10^{7}$ candidate qLDPC codes using approximately $10^{5}$ distance-estimation trials per code, or approximately $10^{12}$ trials in total, as a function of code size. Dark bars show sQetch running on a single GPU; light bars show the state-of-the-art CPU baseline QDistRnd [106]. sQetch completes the full workload in under one week at every size shown, whereas QDistRnd requires years at approximately $100$ data qubits and millennia at approximately $2000$ data qubits. The resulting speedup is of order $10^{5}\times$ and increases with system size.*

The workloads in Figure 7 reflect a realistic search. Good CSS codes are extremely sparse in their natural design spaces. For the lifted-product family with a fixed group, base-matrix shape, and check weight, only a fraction between $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-3}$ of the candidates that survive inexpensive classical prefilters have a useful distance. One must therefore sample on the order of $10^{6}$ – $10^{7}$ candidates to find good codes reliably. For each candidate, the probability that a single random-ISD trial finds a minimum-weight logical operator is of a comparable order, motivating a budget of approximately $10^{5}$ trials per code. The resulting total of approximately $10^{12}$ trials is therefore the natural scale of one discovery run. At this scale, sQetch reduces a computation that would require years to millennia of QDistRnd CPU time to a few GPU-days, making the automated pipeline of Appendix F practical.

### E Hook-error-free syndrome extraction

A fixed pair of check matrices $H_{X}$ and $H_{Z}$ can be implemented by many orderings of the two-qubit gates in a syndrome-extraction (SE) cycle. The ordering matters because a fault on an ancilla can propagate through subsequent gates to several data qubits, producing a hook error. If the resulting spacetime fault is undetected and flips a logical observable, it can reduce the circuit-level distance.

In a mitten code, a ring entry such as $a=g_{1}+g_{2}+g_{3}$ in the check matrices of Eq. 146 corresponds to three separate group-element layers. On an atom-array platform, each layer associated with a group element $g_{i}$ is implemented by a permutation (Section J.A.1). We therefore preserve the group-element layers instead of applying an arbitrary Tanner-graph coloring, and search only over their order in the SE cycle. Each of the $X$ - and $Z$ -check halves contains $12$ layers: six left-regular layers acting on the data blocks $D_{1},\ldots,D_{4}$ and six right-regular layers acting on $D_{5}$ . To minimize the SE-cycle time, we keep the left- and right-regular sections separate and permute only the six group-element layers within each section.

For each candidate ordering, we compile a two-round memory circuit with Stim [80] and extract its detector-error model. We convert this model into a spacetime check/logical pair $(H,L)$ : columns correspond to circuit fault mechanisms, rows of $H$ encode detector parities, and rows of $L$ indicate which logical observables each mechanism flips. A fault pattern $e$ is undetected when $He=0$ and is harmful when, in addition, $Le\neq 0$ . We use sQetch to estimate the distance of this spacetime code, which is the circuit-level distance of the memory experiment, and discard schedules with low estimated distance. Because the spacelike logical operators of the spacetime code include the logical operators of the underlying quantum code, the circuit-level distance is upper-bounded by the code distance. We find distance-preserving schedules for all mitten codes except the $\llbracket 150,30,10\rrbracket$ code. For that code, the best schedule contains weight- $8$ fault patterns in both the $X$ and $Z$ blocks, giving $d_{\mathrm{circ}}=8<10$ . The exact schedules and corresponding SE-cycle visualizations are available in Ref. [61]. Further details of the schedule search are given in Table 8.

## Appendix I Decoding

In this section, we describe our telescoping decoder and provide additional details on how we performed our memory and surgery simulations. We also compare the performance of our decoder to the current state-of-the-art decoders for qLDPC codes and perform a worst-case analysis to demonstrate the capability of our decoder to support sub-millisecond real-time decoding when ported over to FPGAs.

### A Telescoping decoder construction

Our decoding infrastructure is designed to meet two requirements. First, we want to understand the best logical error rates mitten codes can achieve down to the low logical error rate (LER) regime. This requires many Monte Carlo samples and hence a decoding pipeline with high throughput. Second, we want these estimates to reflect a realistic decoding stack that in principle can be optimized to enable real-time decoding. To satisfy both, we adopt a telescoping design [84, 51, 86, 85] in which fast, high-throughput decoders handle the vast majority of shots, and progressively more expensive decoders are invoked only on the small residual of hard shots that earlier tiers defer.

Concretely, our telescoping decoder consists of four stages. The first two run on the GPU, using custom CUDA kernels [119] that implement layered variants of belief propagation (BP) and Relay BP [83]; by decoding large batches of shots concurrently, these stages absorb the vast majority of the Monte Carlo samples at high throughput. The third stage runs on the CPU, using custom C kernels that implement serial variants of BP and Relay-BP, and is applied only to the harder shots the GPU tiers defer. The final stage solves the most-likely-error (MLE) decoding problem through integer programming with Gurobi [120], and is reserved for the hardest shots that all belief-propagation stages leave undecided. Across all of our decoding experiments we construct the full correlated $XYZ$ detector-error model (DEM), but each stage decodes the representation of this model best suited to its role in our telescoping design. One representation restricts the decoding graph to the initialization-basis detectors, giving a much smaller graph and hence higher throughput. The other is the GARI transform [87], which adds auxiliary error and check nodes to remove the short cycles that $Y$ errors induce. We find this improves BP convergence and lowers the LER, and although GARI increases the number of nodes, it reduces the number of edges in the decoding graph by roughly a factor of three for our codes. This selective choice of decoding graph per stage is a key feature of our design that lets us trade off between throughput and accuracy without altering the decoders themselves. We now describe each of the stages in more detail.

Stage 1 (GPU BP). Stage 1 $(S_{1})$ decodes the initialization-basis restriction of the detector-error model. We tune it for maximum convergence without introducing logical errors. Depending on the code and the decoding experiment, between $80\%$ and $99.6\%$ of all shots converge in this stage for physical error rates less than or equal to $p=0.2\%.$ Every shot receives the same fixed number of BP iterations, after which we check for convergence. The first few iterations use the exact sum-product update and the remainder use the cheaper min-sum approximation. We find that this improves convergence and is worth the extra cost of needing to invoke the GPU’s special function unit for the sum-product updates. Within each iteration the message updates are layered. BP passes messages between the check nodes (detectors) and the error nodes of the decoding graph. We partition the check nodes into groups, and each group, together with the error nodes its checks touch, forms a layer. All checks within a layer update in parallel from the same current beliefs. After the layer, the error nodes it touched refresh their beliefs, so the next layer acts on updated information. A fully serial schedule, which updates one check at a time, converges marginally better on our codes but cannot exploit the parallelism of the GPU as effectively as the layered schedule. For circuit-level memory experiments on the $\llbracket 150,30,10\rrbracket$ mitten code and the $\llbracket 144,12,12\rrbracket$ gross code [50] we are able to process over a million rounds of syndrome extraction per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU in this stage.

Stage 2 (GPU Relay-BP). Stage 2 $(S_{2})$ decodes the GARI transform [87] of the detector-error model with a layered version of Relay-BP [83]. Relay-BP augments BP with a memory term that blends each error node’s fixed channel prior with its earlier beliefs. We run many BP legs in sequence. Each leg warm-starts this memory from the beliefs the previous leg ended on, but it restarts message passing from scratch and draws a fresh memory strength for every error node. The strength is signed so it may pull a node’s belief back toward the warm start or push it away. This randomness helps convergence; a shot that stalls in one leg can often converge in a later one. To minimize the logical error rate, we operate this stage with a quorum. A converged leg votes for the logical class corresponding to its candidate correction and we only accept the decoding result when the first $q$ converged legs cast the same vote. Otherwise, we defer to the later CPU stages. The quorum helps protect against BP convergences to the wrong logical class.

Stage 3 (CPU serial BP). Stage 3 $(S_{3})$ receives the small residual of hard shots that the GPU stages defer. With few shots left, throughput matters less than convergence, so this stage runs on CPUs and uses the fully serial BP schedule. Checks update one at a time, and each update sees the beliefs refreshed by all the updates before it. The stage is split into three substages of increasing depth, all decoding the GARI transform [87] of the full correlated $XYZ$ detector-error model. A shot proceeds to the next substage only if the previous one fails to decode it.

$S_{3A}$ runs plain serial BP over a small ensemble of variants that perturb the channel priors, scaling them up or down or adding per-node random noise. The first variant to converge is accepted.

$S_{3B}$ runs a serial version of Relay-BP over various choices of perturbed priors. As in $S_{2}$ , we use a quorum acceptance rule: we accept a class once $q$ converged legs vote for it. However, unlike $S_{2}$ , where the first $q$ collected legs must be unanimous, the legs of all variants here accumulate in one shared tally, and the first class to reach $q$ votes is accepted even if other converged legs dissent.

$S_{3C}$ runs serial BP for many more iterations than any previous stage over a much wider array of prior perturbations. We accept the first converged correction since the goal of this stage is to converge as many of the remaining shots in order to minimize the number that make it to the integer programming stage ( $S_{4}$ ). At low physical error rates, we never observe a logical error at this stage, with most logical errors coming from $S_{2}$ or $S_{3B}$ .

Stage 4 (Integer Programming) Stage 4 $(S_{4})$ decodes the few shots that survive every BP stage by solving the most likely error decoding problem exactly through integer programming using Gurobi [120]. To minimize the size of the problem, we initially only use the initialization basis detectors. We give each shot one CPU hour running on a single CPU core and if the solver times out before solving to optimality, we accept its solution as long as the relative mixed integer programming optimality gap (MIPGap [121]) is less than $0.1$ . At high physical error rates, a non-negligible amount of shots reach the timeout with a gap greater than $0.1$ and we simply count these as logical errors. At low physical error rates, a negligible fraction of shots reach the timeout (at $p=0.1\%$ on the $\llbracket 300,60,14\rrbracket$ mitten code only $3$ out of $7.522$ billion reach the timeout) and for these we employ the following strategies to quickly solve them after the timeout:

- 1. For the memory experiments at the lowest physical error rate probed for each code, we re-decode each timed-out shot on a sub-DEM before elevating to the full correlated $XYZ$ detector error model. The sub-DEM restricts the full $XYZ$ model to the neighborhood of the shot’s triggered detectors. It keeps every error mechanism that touches a triggered detector, and every detector those mechanisms touch. We solve this much smaller problem with a timeout of a few hundred seconds and accept its solution if the MIPGap is below $0.2$ . Otherwise, we promote the shot to the full $XYZ$ model for the remaining hour, accepting at a MIPGap below $0.1$ . All of these solves run on a single CPU core and this strategy is sufficient to solve all remaining shots.

- 2. For the surgery experiments, we simply re-solve the same problem on the initialization-basis detectors with Gurobi parallelized across multiple CPU cores. This dramatically reduces the time to solve to optimality, with all previously timed-out shots converging in tens of seconds to a few minutes at most.

### C Real-time decoding

A real-time decoder faces two distinct requirements. The first is a rate requirement: to avoid the backlog problem [81], the decoder must decode syndromes at least as fast as the processor produces syndrome data. Our decoding stack as described already meets this requirement on any hardware platform, since parallel window decoding [82] allows adding compute to each stage of the pipeline until the amortized decoding time per window falls below the syndrome extraction cycle time. The second is a latency requirement, which emerges when the circuit contains feedforward operations. An operation conditioned on a decoded logical measurement outcome cannot be scheduled until one specific window is decoded. What matters here is the reaction time, the time to decode that single window.

In this section, we perform a worst-case analysis of both requirements on neutral atom quantum processors, assuming a syndrome extraction cycle time of $T_{\mathrm{cyc}}=$1\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}$$ . We show that a single dedicated decoder per stage sustains even the most demanding commitment schedule and that the average reaction time is nevertheless below $T_{\mathrm{cyc}}$ , with its full distribution across stages given in Table 10. We consider an implementation that processes windows one at a time, with the belief propagation (BP) stages running on FPGAs and the integer programming stage parallelized across multiple CPU cores. The FPGA timing is extrapolated from the BP implementations of Refs. [127, 128].

We assume a sliding-window decoder [82] that processes a window of $W=\mathcal{O}(d)$ rounds of syndrome extraction at a time. In the most demanding mode, the window advances by only one round each time, so the decoder must complete one full window decode every syndrome extraction cycle. This is the worst-case commitment schedule: it maximizes the required decode rate, and committing a wider region less often would only reduce this rate. The reaction time, by contrast, is the duration of a single window decode, set by the decode times of the stages that window traverses, and is unaffected by the commitment schedule. We adopt this worst-case commitment assumption throughout and hence never amortize the cost of a window decode over its $\mathcal{O}(d)$ rounds.

Our telescoping decoder maps onto this requirement stage by stage. We assume each stage has its own hardware so that windows that reach later stages do not hold up incoming windows. Let $f_{i}$ be the fraction of syndrome rounds whose window reaches stage $i$ , with $f_{S_{1}}=1$ , and let $t_{i}$ be the worst-case time of one stage- $i$ window decode. A dedicated decoder for stage $i$ keeps up with the incoming syndromes when the utilization ratio

$$ \rho_{i}\;=\;\frac{f_{i}\,t_{i}}{T_{\mathrm{cyc}}}\;<\;1. $$

We now extrapolate what the per-iteration times of the BP stages would be on an FPGA for memory and surgery on mitten codes. We focus on the $\llbracket 200,40,12\rrbracket$ and $\llbracket 300,60,14\rrbracket$ codes for memory and on the $\llbracket 540,108,18\rrbracket$ code for $XX$ surgery, all at $p=0.1\%$ physical error rate. We base our extrapolation on the numbers measured in the FPGA implementations of Refs. [127, 128] which focus on the $\llbracket 144,12,12\rrbracket$ gross code memory. The implementation of Ref. [128] lays out the entire decoding graph on the FPGA. Every check node and error node has its own processing unit, and the edges of the graph are physical wires between them. All nodes compute at once in a flooding BP manner, with one flooding BP iteration taking $24\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ when using detectors only from one basis. The decoder of Ref. [127] instead focuses on the GARI decoding graph. It operates in a serial BP manner, processing one detector check per clock cycle while small parallel units handle the auxiliary consistency checks alongside the serial sweep. One full iteration, where every check is updated once, takes $6.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s}$ with each individual check update taking $3.647\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ .

We time each of our stages with the FPGA implementation that processes the same kind of decoding graph. Ref. [128] decodes the $X$ and $Z$ detector families separately, and its $24\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ figure is measured on those single-family decoding graphs. These are the same kind of decoding graphs that we use in $S_{1}$ of the memory experiments and in every BP stage of the $\llbracket 540,108,18\rrbracket$ surgery experiment. The serial timing applies to the stages that decode the GARI transform, $S_{2}$ and $S_{3}$ of the memory experiments. The final stage $S_{4}$ is not extrapolated at all; we benchmark its timing directly on a 32 CPU core machine.

The gross-code graph is smaller than ours, so we must scale the $24\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ figure up. To do so, we keep the circuit size fixed and stream the larger graph through it in several passes, each pass processing one chunk of gross-code size. The per-iteration time is set by the number of passes an iteration needs:

$$ t_{\mathrm{iter}}\;=\;$24\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$\times N_{\mathrm{pass}}, $$

where $N_{\mathrm{pass}}$ depends on the size of our decoding graph and on the BP schedule. Our stages do not run flooding BP but rather layered or fully serial schedules. For the layered stages, a pass cannot span two layers, because the beliefs must refresh between them, so each layer needs a whole number of passes and an iteration whose layer $k$ carries $E_{k}$ edges takes

$$ N_{\mathrm{pass}}\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\lceil\frac{E_{k}}{E_{\mathrm{gross}}}\right\rceil\;\leq\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\frac{E_{k}}{E_{\mathrm{gross}}}+1\right)\;=\;F+K $$

passes where $K$ is the total number of layers and $F=E/E_{\mathrm{gross}}$ , where $E$ is the edge count of our decoding graph and $E_{\mathrm{gross}}=30{,}672$ is the edge count of the gross-code single-family graph on which the $24\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ was measured.1212 12 Ref. [128] does not report the number of edges in the decoding graph, so we rebuilt it from the depth-7 syndrome extraction circuits of Ref. [50]. In all of our decoding experiments, we have $E_{k}<0.3\cdot E_{\mathrm{gross}}$ so we may take $N_{\mathrm{pass}}=K$ .

Streaming a graph through a fixed circuit works because the structure of the graph can live in memory instead of wiring: the beliefs and messages sit in on-chip memory banks, and address tables tell each processing unit what to read on each pass. This approach pays additional overheads the hard-wired measurement does not: address logic, memory access, and possibly a slower clock. We do not model these; instead we rely on having sufficient margin in our worst case analysis. Most stages extrapolated from the $24\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ number sit at utilization ratios below $0.05$ and would survive a twentyfold overhead; the busiest, the surgery $S_{2}$ stage at $\rho=0.24$ , still survives a fourfold overhead (see Table 10).

For the serial BP stages, the per-iteration time is the number of detector checks in the window times the $3.647\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ clock. The $\llbracket 200,40,12\rrbracket$ and $\llbracket 300,60,14\rrbracket$ windows have $1920$ and $3360$ detector checks, giving $7.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s}$ and $12.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s}$ per iteration. Even though the $\llbracket 540,108,18\rrbracket$ surgery experiment only uses one basis of detectors, we adopt the same $3.647\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$ per check update timing. It has $5112$ detector checks which gives $18.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s}$ per iteration.

We use worst-case iteration counts throughout. $S_{1}$ always runs its full fixed budget: $10$ iterations for the memory experiments and $30$ for the surgery experiment. For $S_{2}$ , we include the warm-up leg and all $40$ relay legs with no early stopping, for $2520$ iterations in total ( $2480$ for surgery). For the $S_{3}$ substages, we include all iterations of every variant: $500$ iterations for $S_{3A}$ , $24{,}480$ for $S_{3B}$ , and $79{,}500$ for $S_{3C}$ . Most shots do not use the maximum allotted iterations in every stage, so extrapolations based on these totals are conservative upper bounds.

Finally, for the integer-programming stage, we directly benchmark rather than extrapolate. We collected the actual shots that reached $S_{4}$ and re-solved them with Gurobi parallelized across $32$ CPU cores, requiring only for the MIPGap [121] to fall below $0.1$ . Accepted solves are fast, with mean times of $5$ to $8\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ and a worst accepted solve of about a minute, with all shots we tested giving the correct logical correction.
